report.headline: Usage projected to fall from 26.6% in the EuroLeague to 20.4% in the NBA — essentially league-average — while the shooting-efficiency projection carries no signal at all.

projection.text: The model projects a usage rate of 20.4% in the NBA, down from 26.6% in the source EuroLeague season, landing almost exactly on the NBA's minutes-weighted average usage of 20.1%.

risks.text: A 16.8% turnover rate in the source season could be a bigger liability if paired with a diminished playmaking role in the NBA.
The true shooting projection of 56.0% is not usable evidence: the model underperforms a simple league-average guess on this metric (4.5% error vs. 4.3% for the baseline).
The usage projection, while better than a trivial baseline, still carries an 80% interval spanning 14.8% to 26.0%, meaning the model can say the role will likely shrink but not price it precisely.
The source season itself was a fairly thin sample of 970 minutes across 31 games, which is the base the projection is built from.

strengths.text: The subject carried an elite offensive role in the EuroLeague, with usage standing 1.26 standard deviations above the league average.
Playmaking numbers were strong: a 29.3% assist rate and 6.162 assists per 75 possessions.
Scoring efficiency in the source season was essentially at the EuroLeague average on a true shooting basis (59.1%, +0.01 sd), despite a heavy shot-creation role.
A high share of shot attempts (56.8%) came from three, suggesting a shot profile suited to spacing in a reduced role.

uncertainty.text: The 80% prediction interval for usage runs from 14.8% to 26.0%, a span of more than two standard deviations of NBA usage (5.6%), covering everything from a bench-level role to a clear high-usage role; the true shooting projection should not be trusted at all, since the model's 4.5% error is worse than the 4.3% error of simply guessing the league average.
